episodes.description: Stirring music plays as we see Leah Meddaoui’s illustrations for Nicola Ranson’s memoir, A Slice of Orange come to life. A thorny vine grows around a girl with a rabbit who turns into a blissful Indian dancer and then a security guard in a booth as black patrol cars enter the scene with threatening sirens. The text asks how did my journey from love to surveillance take place and we see glowing reviews for the book.

episodes.title: How Cult Trauma Impacts Healing: A Cult Survivor Turned Therapist | Unspun Podcast
episodes.description:
#mentalhealth #healing #podcast #cult #cultawareness #sliceoforangememoir #nicolaranson

For 10 years, I was a disciple of the guru, Bhagwan Shree Rajneesh (AKA Osho), from India to Oregon until the commune collapsed amid criminal activity. 

I became a somatic psychotherapist specialising in trauma and have worked with many cult survivors. Nicola taught Counselling Psychology for 17 years as an adjunct faculty member at National University. 

Be sure to like, share, and support the Unspun Podcast!

About A Slice of Orange:

In A Slice of Orange: loving and leaving the Osho/Rajneesh cult (Unsolicited Press, 12/26), Ranson delivers a deeply personal account of her experiences inside the commune, offering a raw exploration of cult indoctrination and the power of coercive control—topical in today’s polarized world.

Her story begins with immigration from England, followed by a strict Canadian convent school, which leads her to seek freedom and adventure in the counterculture. A traumatic experience in the Sahara severs her ties to family, propelling her toward transcendence through magic, theatre, and ultimately the teachings of Bhagwan Shree Rajneesh. 

Immersed in the guru’s radical vision, she travels from India to Oregon, embracing an open marriage and the commune’s spiritual ideals—until paranoia and criminality arise. 

Now a psychotherapist, Ranson uses her expertise to examine how easily we all fall under the sway of influence and control. Her story is a tale of reckoning, resilience and recovery. With the book’s publication in Oregon, she offers a personal act of reconciliation for the harm inflicted by the cult in the 1980s.
